label: Angles, Limits, Cones and Joins
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 184 through 192. We assemble tangent-like data from a metric space: the Alexandrov angle between geodesics, the space of directions, the tangent cone, and the cone and join constructions. Everything follows from comparison angles measured in model spaces.

label: Comparison Angle
notes: Before defining the true angle we measure the comparison angle of a triangle by building its model triangle in the Euclidean plane and reading the Euclidean angle at the chosen vertex. The law of cosines gives an explicit formula, so comparison angles are concrete numbers we can compute from three distances.

label: The Alexandrov Angle
notes: The Alexandrov angle between two geodesics issuing from a point is the limit superior of comparison angles of the small triangles cut off as both parameters shrink to zero. This upper limit always exists, lies between zero and pi, and captures the infinitesimal opening between the two directions.

label: Properties of the Angle
notes: The Alexandrov angle satisfies the triangle inequality among three geodesics from a point, so it behaves like an honest pseudometric on directions. It is also upper semicontinuous in the endpoints, which is exactly the regularity needed to pass to limits and to control how angles vary along families of geodesics.

label: Angles in CAT(k) Spaces
notes: In a CAT(k) space comparison angles are monotone: as the points slide toward the vertex the comparison angle does not decrease, so the limit superior is a genuine limit. The Alexandrov angle then equals the comparison angle of the model triangle, and angle sums of triangles are no larger than their model values.

label: Space of Directions
notes: Two geodesics from a point are equivalent when the angle between them is zero. The Alexandrov angle descends to a metric on equivalence classes; completing this pseudometric space yields the space of directions, written as the link of the point. It records all infinitesimal directions in which one can leave the point.

label: The Tangent Cone
notes: The tangent cone at a point is the Euclidean cone over the space of directions. Points are formal pairs of a direction and a non-negative radius, with the apex collapsing all zero-radius pairs. This is the metric analogue of the tangent space and is the natural place to do infinitesimal geometry.

label: The Euclidean Cone
notes: Given any metric space Y of diameter at most pi we build the Euclidean cone by adding a radial coordinate and gluing all points at radius zero to a single apex. The cone distance comes from the spherical law of cosines using the Y-distance as the angular separation between two rays.

label: Cones and CAT(0)
notes: Berestovskii's theorem is the structural payoff: the Euclidean cone over Y is a CAT(0) space if and only if Y itself is a CAT(1) space. Curvature of the cone is therefore completely governed by curvature of its link, turning a global condition into a condition on directions.

label: The Spherical Join
notes: The spherical join of two spaces sews them together by spherical right triangles, parametrising a join point by an angle between zero and pi over two together with a point in each factor. The join distance is again given by a spherical cosine formula. It is the link-level analogue of an orthogonal direct sum.

label: Joins and CAT(1)
notes: The spherical join of two CAT(1) spaces is again CAT(1). Combined with the cone theorem this lets us build curvature-controlled spaces compositionally: spheres are iterated joins of points, and links of cell complexes are joins, so the join theorem certifies non-positive curvature of large constructions.

label: Limits of Spaces
notes: Ultralimits and Gromov-Hausdorff limits let sequences of CAT(k) spaces converge to a limit space that is again CAT(k). The tangent cone is itself such a limit, the rescaling limit of the space about a point. Limits, angles, cones, and joins thus form one connected toolkit for tangent geometry.
